source.lineage: Compositional ambient emerged where post-minimalist concert writing met ambient production, from Harold Budd and Gavin Bryars in the late 1970s through Max Richter, Ólafur Arnalds, Nils Frahm and Hania Rani after 2000 — slow through-written string and piano writing in diatonic or Aeolian modes, notated parts rather than loops, close-miked felted piano with audible mechanism, long convolution and plate reverb tails, and pieces of 4-12 minutes built on gradual additive layering.

extras.description: Compositional ambient is ambient music written out rather than generated or looped, sitting between post-minimalist concert composition and studio ambient production. Scored piano and string ensemble parts move slowly through modal diatonic harmony, captured with close small-diaphragm miking that keeps felt, hammer and bow noise audible, then placed in long artificial reverb. It is distinguished from generative and drone ambient by having discrete notated events, phrase structure and through-composed form, and from concert minimalism by its studio-built spatial signature and record-length pieces.

extras.description: The jazz saxophone tradition is the improvising lineage that made the tenor and alto the primary solo voices of American jazz from the 1930s onward. extras.description: Dinner jazz is the functional low-dynamic branch of small-group jazz developed for hotel dining rooms and supper clubs, consolidated in the 1950s around the piano trio and the light-toned tenor. source.name: New Age
source.lineage: Contemplative instrumental music codified in California, Japan and Ireland between 1975 and 1990 through Steven Halpern's untempered keyboard drones, Kitarō's synth-and-flute suites and Windham Hill's acoustic roster — slow or unmeasured pulse, consonant diatonic and pentatonic harmony, long-decay reverb, sustained analog pads and string machines, wordless vocal layering, and near-total avoidance of dissonance or backbeat.

extras.description: An instrumental genre built from the mid-1970s around meditation, healing and relaxation contexts rather than concert or dance use, spanning synthesizer suites, solo acoustic playing and world-instrument pastiche. Where ambient proper is often texturally austere or process-driven, new age is melodically explicit and emotionally directive, and unlike minimalism it avoids rigorous structural procedure entirely.

source.name: Jazz Piano (trio and solo idiom)
source.lineage: The piano-led American jazz idiom codified between the 1930s and 1960s by Art Tatum, Bud Powell, Bill Evans, and Thelonious Monk — left-hand rootless voicings and shell chords under a right-hand bebop line, swung eighths at anywhere from ballad rubato to 300 BPM, walking bass and brushed or ride-led drums in the trio format, and improvisation over 32-bar AABA standards and blues.

extras.description: Jazz piano as a distinct performance tradition runs from Harlem stride through Tatum's virtuoso arpeggiation to the Powell-Evans conception of the piano trio as three equal conversational voices, consolidated in the New York and Englewood Cliffs sessions of 1955-1965. Its defining sound is extended tertian harmony voiced rootlessly in the left hand, a horn-derived single-note right-hand line, and interactive bass and brush work rather than timekeeping accompaniment. It differs from stride and boogie-woogie in abandoning the metronomic striding left hand, and from later fusion keyboard playing in staying acoustic and tied to the standard-repertoire chorus form.

source.name: Japanese soundtrack scoring
source.lineage: Japanese screen and game scoring consolidated from the 1950s onward — Toru Takemitsu's sparse modernist film scores for Kobayashi and Teshigahara, Joe Hisaishi's minimalist ostinato-and-melody writing for Miyazaki from 1984, Ryuichi Sakamoto's synth-and-orchestra hybrids, and the game lineage of Koichi Sugiyama and Nobuo Uematsu whose chiptune themes were later rescored for full orchestra — built on long-breathed diatonic or yo-scale themes, ostinato piano or harp figuration, restrained rubato, and orchestral colour weighted toward strings, woodwind solos and celesta.

extras.description: Japanese soundtrack scoring is the composed screen music of Japanese cinema, anime and video games, running from Takemitsu's postwar modernism through Hisaishi's Ghibli scores to the orchestral game repertoire now performed in concert halls. Its recurring traits are a strong, singable principal theme stated and restated over a repeating accompaniment figure, transparent orchestration that leaves individual instrumental colours audible, and pentatonic or modal inflections folded into otherwise Western tonal harmony. Compared with Hollywood scoring it is thinner in texture, less driven by brass, and far more willing to leave silence and single-line writing exposed.

source.name: Chamber Music
source.lineage: Western art-music practice of one player per part for small rooms, standardized between Haydn's Op. 33 quartets (1781) and the Beethoven-Schubert generation and extended by Brahms, Debussy, Bartók and Shostakovich — string quartet, piano trio, quintet and wind serenade formats, fully notated sonata-cycle movements, tempi from grave adagio to presto finales, motivic dialogue traded between equal parts, and a dynamic and articulation vocabulary calibrated to a salon or shoebox hall rather than an orchestra pit.

extras.description: Chamber music is the repertoire written for small ensembles playing without a conductor, one instrument to a line, which Haydn's quartets established as the discipline's central testing ground for motivic development. Against orchestral music it trades mass for transparency and rhetorical intimacy; against solo recital repertoire it is fundamentally conversational, with thematic material passed between equal partners.

source.name: Sonata (Classical Instrumental Form)
source.lineage: Instrumental genre and formal principle consolidated in Vienna and Mannheim between about 1750 and 1830 by C. P. E. Bach, Haydn, Mozart, Clementi and Beethoven, in which a multi-movement work for solo keyboard or solo instrument with keyboard opens with an exposition presenting contrasting first and second themes in tonic and dominant, develops them through remote keys, and recapitulates both in the tonic, typically followed by a slow movement, a minuet or scherzo, and a rondo or sonata-rondo finale.

extras.description: The Classical sonata is chamber-scale instrumental music organized around tonal departure and return: an exposition that establishes a key and then contradicts it, a development that destabilizes both themes through modulation and fragmentation, and a recapitulation that resolves everything into the home key. Textures are lean, usually one or two players, with dynamics articulating structure rather than mood. It is distinguished from the symphony and concerto by its intimate forces and from Baroque suite movements by its dramatic, thematically argued architecture rather than dance-derived binary form.

source.name: Furniture Music (musique d'ameublement)
source.lineage: Coined and composed by Erik Satie with Darius Milhaud in Paris 1917-1923, first performed at the Galerie Barbazanges in 1920 — short modal cells for small mixed ensemble (piano, clarinet, trombone, strings) repeated unchanged for the duration of an interval, deliberately unresolving, dynamically flat and written to be ignored, with Satie shouting at the audience to keep talking.

extras.description: Musique d'ameublement is Satie's early-twentieth-century proposal for music as literal furnishing: brief notated cells for chamber ensemble looped without development for as long as the social occasion lasts, with flat dynamics and no cadential resolution. Titles like Tapisserie en fer forge and Tenture de cabinet prefectoral name domestic objects rather than musical forms. It anticipates ambient music by six decades but differs from it in medium and means — it is fully notated for acoustic players and depends on human repetition rather than tape loop, synthesis or studio process.

source.name: March (concert and military band)
source.lineage: The European and American wind-band march, standardized in 19th-century military service bands and codified for the concert stage by John Philip Sousa's US Marine Band from 1880 and by Kenneth Alford in Britain — duple time at 112-120 BPM, an unvarying alternating-bass snare-and-bass-drum tread, multi-strain AABBCC form with a modulating trio and a piccolo or cornet obbligato descant, scored for cornets, clarinets, low brass, and sousaphone with no strings.

extras.description: The concert and military march is the core repertoire of the wind band, fixed in its modern form by Sousa's Marine Band arrangements of the 1880s-1900s and by British bandmasters such as Kenneth Alford. It is fully notated, strictly duple, and built on a rigid multi-strain plan — introduction, two repeated strains, then a softer trio in the subdominant that returns fortissimo with piccolo descant and a break-strain — over a metronomic bass-drum-and-snare tread. It differs from the brass-band contest repertoire of northern England in its inclusion of clarinets and saxophones, and from processional street music such as second line or banda in its complete absence of improvisation and its fixed European harmonic vocabulary.
exemplars: John Philip Sousa - 'The Stars and Stripes Forever'

source.name: Cape Jazz
source.lineage: South African jazz idiom formed in District Six and the Cape Flats from the late 1950s, codified by Abdullah Ibrahim, the Blue Notes, Robbie Jansen and Basil Coetzee — mid-tempo 4/4 with a lilting ghoema carnival rhythm and marabi-derived cyclic I-IV-V vamps, hymn-like piano voicings from Cape Malay and mission-church singing, penny-whistle and alto-sax lead lines, and an anthemic, deliberately communal ensemble sound.

extras.description: Cape jazz emerged in Cape Town's District Six from the late 1950s, fusing American bebop with marabi's three-chord cycle, the ghoema drum rhythm of the Cape Malay carnival, and mission-church hymnody; Abdullah Ibrahim's 'Mannenberg' (1974) is its founding statement. It is built on short, repeating diatonic vamps rather than changing standards, with hymnlike block-chord piano, swaying two-beat ghoema propulsion, and long modal saxophone solos over a groove that never resolves away. It is more cyclic and less harmonically restless than American hard bop, and distinct from mbaqanga and township jive in tempo, in its jazz solo language, and in its Cape rather than Witwatersrand rhythmic roots.

source.name: Chamber Jazz
source.lineage: Small-group jazz played with classical restraint, formed in the early 1950s with John Lewis's Modern Jazz Quartet and Jimmy Giuffre's drummerless trios and extended from 1969 by Manfred Eicher's ECM productions in Oslo — soft dynamics, brushes or no drums at all, contrapuntal written passages framing improvisation, vibraphone, clarinet, piano and arco bass timbres, and rubato or slow-modal tempos captured in long natural reverb.

extras.description: Chamber jazz is small-ensemble jazz that borrows the textures, dynamics, and written counterpoint of the classical chamber tradition, initiated by the Modern Jazz Quartet and Jimmy Giuffre in the 1950s and given a lasting recorded identity by ECM from 1969. Its signature is quietness and space: brushed or absent drums, arco and pizzicato bass treated as an equal melodic voice, transparent contrapuntal heads, and engineering by Jan Erik Kongshaug that places instruments in a large, cool, decaying hall. It is distinguished from cool jazz by its formal written architecture rather than merely relaxed phrasing, and from free jazz by strict dynamic control and pre-composed frames even when harmony is left open.

extras.description: Khalījī is the shared popular idiom of Kuwait, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the Emirates, consolidated through Gulf state radio orchestras from the 1950s and 60s and carried into pan-Arab stardom by Talal Maddah, Mohammed Abdu and later Abdallah Al Rowaished and Nawal. Its identifying feature is rhythmic: the syncopated Gulf patterns hit on paired mirwās hand drums and ṭabl with clapping, which pull against an otherwise Egyptian-style ensemble of oud, qānūn and unison violin section playing quarter-tone maqām lines. Against Egyptian ṭarab it is shorter-formed, faster and drum-forward; against the older sawt tradition it is orchestrated, notated in part, and built for broadcast rather than for the intimate ṣawt majlis.

source.name: Rare Groove
source.lineage: A UK-defined canon rather than a scene of origin: obscure American funk and soul 45s and album cuts from roughly 1969-1976 excavated by London DJs Norman Jay, Judge Jules and the Kiss FM pirate circuit at warehouse parties in 1985-1988 — mid-tempo 90-105 BPM one-chord funk vamps, dry unprocessed drum breaks, clavinet and Rhodes comping, punchy small-section horns, and gritty gospel-shout vocals, all cut fast and cheaply on small independent labels.

extras.description: Rare groove names the body of low-selling early-1970s American funk and soul that London warehouse-party DJs rediscovered in the mid-1980s and turned into a working repertoire, which in turn fed the sample libraries of hip-hop and acid jazz. The typical record is a modestly budgeted, dry-sounding one-chord funk vamp with an exposed drum break, chicken-scratch guitar, and a shouted lead. It is distinguished from mainstream 1970s funk not by musical technique but by obscurity and by the breakbeat-forward, extended-vamp cuts that collectors selected for.
exemplars: Maceo & the Macks - Cross the Tracks

source.name: Brit Funk
source.lineage: British Black dance-band funk of 1978-1984 centred on London's Acton, Wembley and Southall youth-club circuit and the Ealing/Crackers jazz-funk dancefloors, made by Light of the World, Hi-Tension, Freeez, Level 42, Beggar & Co and Incognito — jazz-schooled slap and thumb bass, tight brass sections, Rhodes and Prophet pads, Latin percussion, tempos of 105-120 BPM, and a lighter, more instrumental-led approach than American funk with chanted group vocals.

extras.description: Brit funk was the first substantial British-made Black dance music, produced between the late 1970s and mid-1980s by young London bands who had grown up on imported American jazz-funk records and on the Caribbean sound-system circuit. Its markers are virtuosic slap bass, crisply arranged horn lines, Latin percussion, and long instrumental sections with vocals used as chanted hooks. Compared with contemporaneous American funk it is brighter, jazzier and less vocal-centred, and it fed directly into the UK's later acid jazz and street soul.
exemplars: Light of the World - Round Trip

source.name: Traditional Funk
source.lineage: The foundational funk idiom codified by James Brown's bands at King Records in Cincinnati and on the road between 1965 and 1974 (Jabo Starks, Clyde Stubblefield, Bootsy Collins, Fred Wesley, Maceo Parker) and paralleled by Dyke & the Blazers and the Meters — single-chord vamps with all parts locked to 'the One', sixteenth-note damped guitar, staccato horn punctuation, syncopated melodic bass, and shouted, percussive lead vocals at 95-115 BPM, cut live to tape with minimal overdubs.

extras.description: Traditional funk is the mid-1960s to early-1970s core of the genre, in which R&B song form gave way to extended one-chord vamps with every instrument treated as a percussion part and the downbeat of bar one carrying the accent. James Brown's bands defined the grammar; the Meters and Dyke & the Blazers supplied parallel dialects. It is played live in a room with little studio construction, which separates it from the multitracked, synth-heavy funk of the later 1970s and from P-Funk's psychedelic layering, and its harmonic stasis distinguishes it from the chord-driven soul it grew out of.
exemplars: The J.B.'s - Doing It to Death

extras.description: The dominant European compositional style from roughly 1450 to 1560, exported by singers trained in Cambrai, Bruges and Antwerp to courts and chapels from Rome to Vienna. source.lineage: Codified by Manfred Eicher and engineer Jan Erik Kongshaug at Oslo's Rainbow Studio from ECM's founding in 1969, it is a European chamber-jazz manner — slow to medium tempos, modal or folk-derived material, brushed or mallet-led drums, arco double bass, piano and saxophone recorded with long artificial and room reverb, wide dynamic range, minimal overdubbing and an editorial preference for space over density.

source.name: Contemporary post-bop
source.lineage: Post-1995 New York small-group idiom codified at Smalls and the Village Vanguard by Brad Mehldau, Mark Turner, Kurt Rosenwinkel and Chris Potter — extended-form originals with slow-moving upper-structure harmony, long asymmetric phrase groupings over 4/4 or shifting 5/4 and 7/4, elastic ride-cymbal time and conversational drum interaction, and a soft-attack tenor and nylon-clean guitar timbre far from hard bop's blues declamation.

extras.description: Contemporary post-bop is the acoustic small-group mainstream that consolidated in New York from the mid-1990s onward, descending from the Miles Davis mid-1960s quintet and Wayne Shorter's compositional model rather than from Blue Note hard bop. It is marked by originals with irregular phrase lengths, harmony built from slash voicings and pedal-anchored upper structures, drummers who imply rather than state the pulse, and a deliberately unforced, high-resolution recorded tone. It differs from hard bop by rejecting blues-and-gospel vocabulary as the default rhetoric, and from ECM-school jazz by keeping American swing feel and bebop line-construction at the centre rather than open Nordic space.

source.name: Neo Soul
source.lineage: Philadelphia, New York and Detroit R&B movement of 1995-2005 centered on D'Angelo, Erykah Badu, the Soulquarians and producers James Poyser and J Dilla, marked by live Rhodes-and-bass rhythm sections playing deliberately behind the beat, extended jazz voicings over hip-hop-derived boom-bap drum feels at 70-95 BPM, warm analog tracking, and a conversational, melismatic gospel-rooted vocal delivery layered into dense close-harmony stacks.

extras.description: Neo soul crystallized in the mid-1990s as a reaction against the programmed gloss of contemporary R&B, restoring live band tracking, analog tape warmth and jazz-level harmony while retaining hip-hop's rhythmic sensibility. Its defining sound is the drunk, dragging pocket — drums and bass placed audibly late against the click — over Rhodes and Wurlitzer voicings with ninths, elevenths and passing chromatic movement, topped by intimate, heavily stacked lead vocals. It differs from classic 1970s soul in its hip-hop drum feel and studio-loop construction, and from mainstream 1990s R&B in its refusal of quantized grids and its harmonic ambition.

source.name: Ambient fusion
source.lineage: Ambient-oriented electric improvisation and studio montage, represented by Jon Hassell and Maarifa Street’s Last Night the Moon Came Dropping Its Clothes in the Street (2009). Trumpet, bass, violin and live sampling dissolve the boundary between ensemble performance and electronic soundscape. Hassell’s Fourth World practice is a formative branch of this wider jazz/electronic intersection, not a synonym for every ambient-fusion recording.

extras.description: Ambient fusion places improvised instrumental gestures inside a continuously reworked electronic environment. The selected Hassell/Maarifa Street branch keeps a breath-led trumpet, subdued electric bass, bowed violin and live-sampling layer, with motifs overlapping instead of a solo succession over a driving rock backline. The credited 2009 album combines studio material, live recordings and subsequent montage; this reduced ensemble captures that practice without reproducing every credit. Unlike conventional jazz fusion, percussion and virtuosic attack are secondary; unlike ambient IDM, live melodic improvisation is central. The trumpet articulation, fretless setup and spatial chain are proposed defaults, not documented artist equipment.
